title: Why Do People Gossip? What Research Shows
voiceover: Why do people gossip so much? In 1997, Robin Dunbar and colleagues analyzed 45 natural conversations. About two thirds of the conversation time went to social topics. In 2020, Megan Robbins and Alexander Karan sampled everyday conversations of 467 people. They found gossip was mostly neutral, not negative. On average, it took up about 52 minutes of an awake day. In 2012, Matthew Feinberg and colleagues described sharing reputational information as a form of prosocial behavior. And in 2014, his team reported that gossip and ostracism promote cooperation in groups. These findings come from specific samples and tasks, so they don't describe all gossip. So gossip is common, often neutral, and sometimes helps groups cooperate. Tomorrow: can other people really read how you feel?

In everyday recordings of 467 people, gossip was mostly neutral, and experiments suggest sharing reputational information can be prosocial and can help groups cooperate. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Dunbar, R. I. M., Marriott, A., & Duncan, N. D. C. (1997). Human conversational behavior. Human Nature, 8(3), 231-246. accuracy_note: Findings come from specific samples and tasks (observed conversations, recorded daily speech, lab group games), so they do not describe all gossip. The video does not say gossip is always harmless.
